facts.what_happened: In 1999 the county migrated from an AS/400 green-screen system to a vendor package from Indianapolis.
The conversion brought over account master and current read data but not estimate history.
On compound meters (three-inch and up, commercial accounts), the estimate logic averaged the prior twelve readings on a calendar quarter basis, while billing ran on a rolling sixty-day cycle.

Estimates on affected commercial accounts came in about eleven percent light, then a true-up in February produced bills such as a fourteen-hundred-dollar bill, and customers complained to Doreen at the front desk.
The discrepancy was not caught because staff reviewed the summary page.
The summary page balanced.
The exception register printed on greenbar paper about nine inches thick and was generally not read.
The speaker read the exception register.
The speaker took the register home and reviewed it at the kitchen table at night, while his son Nathan, then a baby, was up at 11 and 2.
The speaker found the pattern.
It took about five or six weeks of Tuesdays to hand-figure roughly forty accounts to prove the pattern.
The speaker wrote up the finding.
The writeup was two pages.
The speaker gave the writeup to Marlene Deemer, the supervisor.
Marlene read the two pages standing up in about two minutes, said "Kovarik, you're the only one in here who actually reads the back page," put it down, and went to lunch.
Marlene died in 2014; the speaker attended her funeral and did not tell her daughter about the incident.
After the incident, the speaker began keeping his own set of books/records: first a Green Bandy notebook, later an Excel workbook.
The workbook grew to include exception logic, compound conversions, and a cross-reference for parcels resplit in an annexation that never received new account numbers.
There are about eleven hundred such resplit parcel accounts.
No one else can run the workbook.
In 2016 the speaker was on vacation in Myrtle Beach with Tammy's family and the office called him on Wednesday morning.
The office called again on Thursday.
The speaker walked the office through the workbook by phone.
He did this twice.
The speaker built a flag in the system that zeroes the late penalty for residential single-occupancy accounts flagged as an older person living alone.
No one instructed him to create this flag.
No one instructed him not to create this flag.

facts.what_happened: Speaker went out on a boat in August 2004, out of Catawba, with brother-in-law Denny, at age 30.
Denny owned a nineteen-foot Lund, approx. 1986, with a 90hp main motor and a 9.9hp kicker motor for trolling.
Denny mixed the kicker's gas by eyeball rather than measuring.
They were fishing about four and a half miles northeast of the reef complex; water conditions were flat/calm.
The kicker motor began loading up.
The kicker motor, a two-stroke, fouled out; they lost about one hour and twenty minutes to the problem.
Speaker pulled both spark plugs and cleaned them using a nail file from Denny's tackle box; they ran the rest of the day on one plug.
They caught seventeen fish.
They kept twelve fish.
The largest fish, seven and a quarter pounds, was caught on Denny's line; speaker netted it.
Denny had been laid off from Cooper Standard around March of that year.
Denny had worked at Cooper Standard for fourteen years.
Karen (speaker's wife's sister) told Tammy that Denny wasn't doing well with the layoff.
Denny was reported to be sitting in the garage.
Tammy told speaker to take Denny out on the boat and let the topic come up if it did.
Speaker agreed.
They were out on the boat for nine and a half hours.
The topic of the layoff did not come up during the trip.
They discussed fishing gear (bottom bouncer vs. crawler harness, weight sizes) for about forty-five minutes, the Indians bullpen, and Denny's father's old Starcraft boat.
Speaker asked Denny if he'd tried drift socks; Denny said no.
Speaker told Denny drift socks cost about thirty dollars at the Dick's in Findlay and would hold the boat to about 1.1 mph.
Denny responded 'huh.'
Denny has worked at the Marathon terminal since 2006.
When they returned to the ramp around 9pm, Denny, not looking up while tying down the boat, said 'We oughta do this every year'; speaker replied 'Absolutely.'
They never repeated the trip together again.
Twenty-two years have passed since the trip.
Over the years, the boat needed a lower unit repair, Karen's mother had a hip issue, and Denny's kids got into soccer.
Denny currently owns a pontoon boat.
Speaker and Denny see each other on Christmas Eve and the Fourth of July.
Denny still does not measure his gas.

facts.what_happened: In 2011 the Supervisor Two, Billing and Customer Accounts position (formerly Marlene's) came open.
Doreen brought the speaker a congratulations card before he applied.
The speaker did not submit an application.

He filled out the application sections (name, dates of service, certifications) in pen at the kitchen table.
Section Six required a half-page written response on supervisory philosophy and an example of addressing a performance issue.
He never wrote in Section Six.
On the deadline day (noon Friday), he drove past the admin building on his lunch break and kept driving.
He went to Arby's.

He told Tammy that night the financial calculation: $4,200/year raise before taxes, about $200/month after PERS pickup and bracket change, loss of overtime eligibility, plus on-call duty for main breaks and Nathan's travel-ball season/Cooperstown trip.
Tammy said okay and did not push.
Brad Nusser, 31, from the engineering side, got the position.
Speaker trained Brad for six weeks.
Brad has been his supervisor for about fifteen years.
Brad brings speaker a Dairy Queen cake on his anniversary date every year.
Around 2014-15, Brad conducted a corrective action on Cheryl Vandersteen (18 years tenure) over time card issues; speaker served as department witness.
The meeting lasted forty minutes in the conference room.
Cheryl cried during the meeting, then returned to her desk and completed her afternoon work.
Speaker still has the application.
The application is in the gray filing cabinet in the garage, second drawer, with snowblower manuals.
Tammy found the application while cleaning the garage; held it up without speaking; speaker said throw it out; she put it back.
The filing cabinet also contains receipts from a Buick sold in 2009.

facts.what_happened: Before working in billing, speaker worked on the meter route.
Speaker read meters for two years, 1995 to 1997, on west side and township route.
A woman named Ardith Bolyard lived on Mulberry, estimated by speaker to be about seventy-eight.
Her meter read came in at approximately ninety-one thousand gallons on a sixty-day cycle; she was a widow living alone in a fourteen-hundred square foot house.
Her normal usage was about four thousand gallons.
The resulting bill, including sewer charges billed off the water read, would have been about eleven hundred dollars.
Speaker specifies the bill as eleven forty or eleven forty-something dollars.
Speaker went to Ardith's house and found the cause was the toilet.
The cause was the flapper.
The flapper was a four-dollar rubber flapper that had gone soft, running silently down the back of the bowl.
Ardith had not heard the leak.
Speaker went to the Hardware on Main on his lunch break, bought a flapper (one dollar ninety-nine) and a chain clip (about two forty), and installed them.
The repair took eleven minutes.
Speaker returned to the truck and entered the read as a meter-fail estimate.
The meter had not actually failed.
The meter was fine.
Speaker typed it as a fail, entered her twelve-month average, the change went through, and she received a forty-one dollar bill; no one raised the issue in thirty years.
Ardith gave speaker a can of Vernors from her fridge.
Speaker did not want the Vernors and does not like it.
Speaker drank it.
Speaker thought about the event for about a year, then wrote a proposal for a leak forgiveness policy: a one-time adjustment to average usage for verified leaks fixed within thirty days.
Speaker typed up the proposal.
Speaker did not put his name on the document.
Speaker gave the document to Ron Mierzwa, saying someone might want to consider it; Ron put his name on it.
The proposal went to the board in 1998 and passed.
Ron received a plaque.
The plaque is at Ron's house; speaker saw it at Ron's retirement event.
Ardith died sometime in the early 2000s.
Her house is now a rental with vinyl siding.
About eleven to twelve hundred accounts per year now go through the adjustment policy.
Speaker looked up the number once.
The number was twelve hundred six in 2019.
Speaker states the repair cost four dollars and thirty-nine cents of his own money, counting the chain clip.
